notes.summary:
A sentence is given with one part underlined (or in bold). You choose the option that makes it correct, or No improvement / No substitution required if it is already correct. SSC asks 1 to 2 in Tier 1 and more in Tier 2.

Method: first decide whether the underlined part is wrong at all. Read the whole sentence, find the rule being tested (tense, conditional, agreement, verb pattern, preposition, comparison, determiner, connector or word choice), then pick the option that fixes that rule and adds no new error. Expect No improvement to be the answer in roughly one question out of five.

concepts.title: How to work through an improvement question
concepts.body:
1. Read the full sentence, not just the underlined part. The error is often a clash with a word outside it (since, if, Hardly).
  2. Name the rule using the list below. Ask: what does this sentence need here?
  3. Predict the correct form before looking at the options.
  4. Eliminate options that add a new error, change the meaning, or are only partly fixed (studying since two o'clock fixes the preposition; study since two o'clock does not fit has been).
  5. Choose No improvement only when the original passes every check, including idiom and style.

concepts.title: Tense and time
concepts.body:
RuleCorrectIncorrect
Action from the past continuing now: present perfect (continuous) + since/forMy friend has been living in a village since 2015.My friend lives in a village since 2015.
since + point of time; for + periodShe has been studying since two o'clock.She has been studying for two o'clock.
Right now: present continuousI'm not wearing sunglasses at the moment.I don't wear sunglasses at the moment.
Opinion, knowledge, liking: simple present (state verbs)I think that tomorrow I will take leave.I am think that tomorrow I will take leave.
Future result of a present condition: willIf you join now, it will prove to be good in the long run.If you join now, it proves to be good in the long run.
Prediction from present evidence: going toThe bus is full; it is going to leave soon.(will leave is acceptable but SSC prefers going to with visible evidence)
Finished past time: simple pastHe left yesterday.He has left yesterday.
Earlier of two past actions: past perfectThe film had started before we arrived.The film started before we had arrived.
Time clause (when, after, before, as soon as) uses present for futureI will call you when I reach.I will call you when I will reach.

concepts.title: Conditionals and wishes
concepts.body:
TypeIf clauseMain clauseExample
Zero (facts)simple presentsimple presentIf you heat ice, it melts.
First (likely future)simple presentwill + V1If it rains, we will stay in.
Second (unreal present)simple past / werewould + V1If I were the Prime Minister, I would build more schools.
Third (unreal past)had + V3would have + V3If he had listened, he would not have fallen ill.
  • Inversion drops if: Had he listened to his doctor, he would not have fallen ill. Were I rich, I would travel. Should you need help, call me.
  • were for all subjects in unreal conditions: If I were you, If she were here.
  • wish about the present takes past; about the past takes past perfect: I wish I knew the answer. I wish I had studied harder.
  • as if / as though for something unreal: He talks as if he were the boss.
  • No would in the if clause: If I had known, not If I would have known.
  • Unless = if not, so no extra not: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.

concepts.title: Subject-verb agreement
concepts.body:
• No one, nobody, everyone, each, every, either, neither are singular: No one is supposed to react. Incorrect: No one are supposed to react.
  • there is / there are follow the noun after them: there are so many misconceptions; there is so much confusion.
  • One of the + plural noun + singular verb: One of my friends lives in Pune.
  • The number of + singular verb; a number of + plural verb.
  • Uncountable nouns take a singular verb: The information was useful.
  • Subjects joined by as well as / with / along with follow the first subject; either ... or / neither ... nor follow the nearer subject.
  • Collective nouns as one unit are singular: The committee has decided.

concepts.title: Infinitive, gerund and verb form
concepts.body:
PatternWordsCorrectIncorrect
to + V1plan, want, decide, hope, agree, refuse, promise, afford, tryI plan to pursue law.I plan to pursuing law.
-ingavoid, enjoy, finish, mind, practise, suggest, give up, can't help, keepShe avoided meeting him.She avoided to meet him.
to as a preposition + -inglook forward to, object to, be used to, be accustomed to, with a view to, devoted toWe look forward to meeting you.We look forward to meet you.
adjective + of + -ingcapable of, confident of, fond of, proud of, afraid of, sure ofHe is capable of doing this work. She is confident of winning.He is capable to do this work.
insist, prevent, succeed + preposition + -inginsist on, prevent from, succeed inShe insisted on my taking the medicine / insisted that I take the medicine.She insisted me to take the medicine.
verb + object + to + V1ask, tell, advise, allow, want, expect, orderHe advised me to rest.He advised me resting.
verb + object + V1 (no to)let, make, help, see, hear, watchLet me go.Let me to go.
Purpose: to + V1after a verb showing purposeWhat examples did the writer give to prove his point?gave to proved his point
Past participle opening (passive meaning)when the subject receives the actionBlinded by a dust storm, they fell into disorder.Blind by a dust storm ...
Main verb neededa sentence needs a finite verbThe old lady nearly died of fright. You can always depend on me.The old lady nearly dead from fright. You can always dependent on me.

concepts.title: Prepositions and collocations
concepts.body:
IncorrectCorrect
apologised the teacherapologised to the teacher
depend over / at medepend on me
different than / then the onedifferent from the one
careless from my cardcareless with my card
tattooed in their skintattooed on their skin
partake this refreshmentpartake of this refreshment
conversed the matter with mediscussed the matter with me
misconception on dyslexiamisconception about dyslexia
died from frightdied of fright

reached to Delhireached Delhi

made fussmade a fuss about
by walkon foot

Common collocations: make a decision, a mistake, progress, a fuss, an effort; do homework, a favour, business, your best; take a break, a decision (also correct), an exam; pay attention, a visit, a compliment; keep a promise, in touch; heavy rain, traffic; strong tea; fast colours; hard-earned money.

concepts.title: Adjectives, adverbs and comparison
concepts.body:
• Comparatives need the comparative form + than: Hritik is slower than Heer. Incorrect: slow than.
  • Long adjectives use more / less: Edward II is less tragic than some other plays. Incorrect: tragic than, as least tragic as.
  • Equality: as ... as; negative equality: not so / not as ... as.
  • No double forms: better, not more better; most beautiful, not most beautifullest.
  • the + superlative + of / in: the tallest boy in the class.
  • the + comparative ..., the + comparative: The harder you work, the better you score.
  • Adverb for a verb: She spoke softly; adjective after linking verbs: The soup tastes good.
  • very with positive degree, much / far with comparatives: much taller, not very taller.
  • Order of adjectives: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose: a beautiful small old round red Indian wooden dining table.

concepts.title: Nouns, pronouns and determiners
concepts.body:
WordUse withCorrectIncorrect
many / few / a few / fewercountable pluralsso many misconceptionsso much misconception
much / little / a little / lessuncountable nounsmuch water, less noisemany water
somepositive sentences and offersCan you give me some more examples?so many examples / some many examples
anynegatives and questionsI don't have any money.I don't have some money.
between / amongtwo / more than twoThe players distributed the reward among themselves.between themselves (for many players)
each other / one anothertwo / more than twoThe two sisters helped each other.The two sisters helped one another.
themselvesreflexive pluralThey hurt themselves.their selves, theirselves
either / neithertwoEither of the two roads.Either of the three roads (use any).
whose / who'spossession / who isThe girl whose bag was lost.The girl who's bag was lost.

Uncountable nouns (advice, information, furniture, luggage, equipment) take no a and no plural: a piece of advice, some information.

concepts.title: Connectors, inversion and word order
concepts.body:
• Hardly / Scarcely / Barely + had + subject + V3 ... when: Hardly had he sat on the chair when it broke. Hardly had we got in when the train started.
  • No sooner + had + subject + V3 ... than: No sooner had I reached than it began to rain.
  • Negative opening words invert: Never have I seen such a sight. Seldom does he smile. Not only did she sing, but she also danced.
  • Indirect question order: inside a statement or another question, use subject + verb: Do you know where she resides? Incorrect: where does she reside, where she reside.
  • while + -ing for two actions at the same time: Let us not neglect important aspects of life while pursuing momentary pleasures.
  • although / though show contrast; do not add but. because / since / as give a reason; so gives a result; unless means if not.
  • Position of only, even, just, often: put it next to the word it limits. He only lent me ten rupees (did nothing else) vs He lent me only ten rupees (no more than ten).
  • Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb and after be: She always arrives early. She is always early.

concepts.title: Word choice and redundancy
concepts.body:
Confusing pairMeaningExample
populous / populatedwith many people / lived ina populous country of 120 million
economic / economicalabout the economy / not wastefuleconomic policy; an economical car
historic / historicalfamous, important / about historya historic win; historical records
childish / childlikesilly / innocentchildlike wonder
alternate / alternativeevery second / another optionon alternate days; an alternative plan
continual / continuousrepeated often / without a breakcontinual interruptions; continuous rain
sensible / sensitivewise / easily affecteda sensible decision; sensitive skin
beside / besidesnext to / in addition tosit beside me; besides English, he knows French
lie / layrest / put down (needs object)lie down; lay the book on the table
rise / raisego up / lift (needs object)prices rise; raise your hand

Redundant words to remove: repeat again, return back, revert back, the reason is because, each and every, cousin brother, past history, free gift, end result, final outcome, still continues to, ascend up.
Correct: The teacher asked the boy to repeat his answer. Incorrect: repeat again.

Fixed expressions: in his own image, on foot, carry out assigned duties, pay heed to, take into account, in spite of (not in spite alone).

concepts.title: When to choose No improvement
concepts.body:
Choose it when the underlined part already follows every rule and reads naturally. Typical correct originals that tempt people to change them:

  • She has been living in Pune for ten years. (present perfect continuous + for: correct)
  • Hardly had we reached the station when the train left. (correct inversion and pair)
  • If I were you, I would apologise. (subjunctive: correct)
  • Neither of the answers is correct. (singular: correct)

Do not pick an option just because it sounds more formal or longer. If the meaning or tense changes, it is not an improvement.

varieties.name: Tense and time
varieties.how: Check time markers (since, for, at the moment, yesterday, if/when) and match the tense; for continuing actions use the present perfect (continuous).

example.q: Improve the underlined part: My friend <u>lives in a village since</u> 2015.
steps: since 2015 shows an action that started in the past and continues.
Simple present lives cannot go with since.
Use present perfect continuous: has been living in a village since.
example.answer: has been living in a village since

varieties.name: Conditionals and wishes
varieties.how: Identify the conditional type from the unchanged clause, then use the matching pair: present/will, past/would, had + V3/would have + V3. Use were in unreal conditions.

example.q: Improve the bold part: Had he listened to his doctor, he will not fall ill.
steps: Had he listened = If he had listened: third conditional (unreal past).
The main clause needs would have + V3.
So would not have fallen.

varieties.name: Subject-verb agreement
varieties.how: Find the subject and check the verb's number. No one, each, every, either, neither are singular; there is/are follows the next noun.

example.q: Improve the underlined part: <u>No one are supposed to react</u> to her prejudiced comments.
steps: No one is singular.
are must become is.
Tense and meaning stay the same.
example.answer: No one is supposed to react

varieties.name: Infinitive, gerund and verb form
varieties.how: Check what the previous word demands: to + V1 after plan/want; -ing after a preposition (look forward to, capable of); V1 after modals and did.

example.q: Improve the bold part: We are looking forward to meet you at the conference.
steps: In look forward to, to is a preposition.
A preposition is followed by a noun or -ing form.
So meeting.

varieties.name: Prepositions and collocations
varieties.how: Recall the fixed preposition for the verb, noun or adjective (apologise to, depend on, different from). Remove prepositions after verbs like discuss and reach.

example.q: Improve the underlined part: The student <u>apologised the teacher</u> for the delay in submitting the assignment.
steps: apologise takes to before the person and for before the fault.
for the delay is already there; to is missing.
Tense (simple past) stays.

varieties.name: Adjectives, adverbs and comparison
varieties.how: If than follows, the adjective must be comparative (-er or more/less). With as ... as, use the plain form.

example.q: Improve the underlined part: Hritik is <u>slow</u> than Heer.
steps: than shows a comparison of two people.
slow is a short adjective, so add -er.
slower than Heer.

varieties.name: Nouns, pronouns and determiners
varieties.how: Check countable vs uncountable (many/much, few/little), some vs any, between (two) vs among (many), each other vs one another, and correct pronoun forms.

example.q: Improve the underlined part: The players distributed the reward <u>between themselves</u>.
steps: The players means more than two people.
among is used for more than two.
themselves is the correct reflexive.

varieties.name: Connectors, inversion and word order
varieties.how: Check the pair (Hardly ... when, No sooner ... than), inversion after negative openers, and statement order inside an indirect question.

example.q: Improve the underlined part: Do you know <u>where does she reside</u>?
steps: where ... is an indirect question inside Do you know.
Indirect questions use statement order with no does.
Third person singular takes resides.

varieties.name: Word choice and redundancy
varieties.how: Remove words that repeat the meaning; pick the word whose exact meaning fits (populous vs populated, on foot vs by walk).

example.q: Improve the bold part: The teacher asked the boy to repeat again his answer.
steps: repeat already means to say again.
again is redundant.
Keep only repeat.

tips: Read the whole sentence before the options; the clue is often outside the underlined part (since, if, Hardly, than).
Predict the correction first, then look for it. This stops tempting but wrong options from steering you.
Reject any option that fixes the error but adds another one, or changes the meaning or tense of the sentence.
If the original passes every check, choose No improvement confidently; SSC uses it as the answer fairly often.
When two options are both grammatical, choose the more natural and concise one; SSC rewards standard idiom.
Learn the gerund-after-to list (look forward to, object to, be used to, with a view to); it appears every year.
Third conditional is the most tested pattern: had + V3 in one clause, would have + V3 in the other.
traps: 'If I was' in an unreal condition is wrong in SSC; use 'If I were'.
Never use would in the if clause: 'If I had known', not 'If I would have known'.
In 'look forward to', 'object to' and 'used to' (meaning accustomed), to is a preposition, so the next verb takes -ing.
Indirect questions do not take do/does/did or question order: 'I wonder where he lives', not 'where does he live'.
Hardly and Scarcely pair with when; only No sooner pairs with than.
A longer or more formal option is not automatically better. Check grammar, not length.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
The teacher asked the boy to repeat again his answer.
questions.solution: Repeat already means 'say again', so again is redundant. Correct: repeat his answer.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
She has been living in Pune for ten years.
questions.solution: for ten years describes an action that started in the past and continues now, so the present perfect continuous has been living is correct. No improvement.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
If I was the Prime Minister, I would build more schools.
questions.solution: For an imaginary present situation, English uses the subjunctive were for all persons: If I were…, I would…

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
We are looking forward to meet you at the conference.
questions.solution: In look forward to, to is a preposition, so it takes a gerund: looking forward to meeting.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
Had he listened to his doctor, he will not fall ill.
questions.solution: Had he listened = If he had listened (type 3, unreal past). The main clause must be would not have fallen.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
Hardly had we reached the station when the train left.
questions.solution: With a negative adverb like Hardly at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject: Hardly had we reached … when. The sentence is already correct.

flashcards.back: If + had + V3, … would have + V3
look forward to meeting — 'to' is a preposition here
If + simple present, ... will + V1: If it rains, we will stay in.
If + simple past (were), ... would + V1: If I had money, I would buy it.
of + -ing: capable of doing, confident of winning
where she resides: statement order inside a question
insist on + -ing, or insist that + subject + V1: She insisted that I take the medicine.
